That is, the soul frequently commands evil; evil here is disobedience. And His words: ﴿except those upon whom my Lord has mercy﴾. It has been said: except those whom my Lord has mercy upon. Here there are two meanings. The first: he pointed to the state of protection (ʿiṣmah) at the sight of the proof (burhan). The second view: "except those upon whom my Lord has mercy" refers to the angels, for Allah the Most High did not place desire in them, and He created them with protection from concern (hamm) and other things.

And His words: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ are clear.

"And the king said, 'Bring him to me that I may take him exclusively for myself.'" Its meaning: I will make him specially mine, so that no one shares him with me. "So when he spoke to him": there is an ellipsis in the verse as well. It is related that the messenger went to him and called him, so he stood up, bathed, put on clean clothes [nidafan], and came to the king. As for His saying, "So when he spoke to him," in the story the king asked him to interpret the dream again so that he could hear it from him directly, and he related it to him. This is the meaning of His saying, "So when he spoke to him." It is also said: the king knew seventy languages of the peoples, so he spoke to Yusuf in those languages, and Yusuf answered him in all of them, and [he added] the tongue of the Hebrew and the Arabic, and the king did not know that. So he said, "Indeed, you are today with us established and trustworthy." Al-makanah (standing) is rank, dignity, and a lofty degree; and His saying "trustworthy" (amin) means truthful.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 55:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land﴾. The scholars differed over why Yusuf, peace be upon him, requested this. Some of them said: he requested it because he knew that it would lead to his family and his brothers and others reaching him from his father and others. Others among them said: he requested it because he knew that he was the most capable of people in managing the affairs of the people during the lean years, so he sought this position for that reason.

As for His saying: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land﴾, "the land" here means the land of Egypt, and the treasuries are the treasuries of food and wealth. Rabi' ibn Anas said: "Set me over the treasuries of the land" means: over the revenue (kharaj) of Egypt and its income.

﴿Indeed, I am a guardian who is knowing﴾, meaning: a guardian of the treasuries, knowing the ways of managing their interests. In some tafsirs: "Indeed, I am a guardian who is knowing" means: a scribe and a reckoner. If it is asked: Is it permissible for a Muslim to take up a task under the hand of a disbeliever?

We say: They have said that if he knows that the disbeliever will leave him free and that the work is conducted in accordance with the truth, then it is permissible for him to take it up. And ﴿Thus We established Yusuf in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾. It is related that the king of Egypt was not a tyrant or an oppressor; rather he was a man chaste in his religion, and the tyrant and oppressor was Pharaoh of Musa. In the narrative: the king waited a year without appointing him, and then he appointed him. And in some strange reports, through the narration of Anas from the Prophet (ﷺ): "If Yusuf had not requested it, he would have appointed him immediately, but when he requested it, he delayed the kingship for a year."

If someone says: Is it permissible for a person to praise himself when Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, I am a guardian who is knowing"?

We say: It is permissible when there is a general benefit in it. It has also been said: it is permissible if he knows that no harm will befall him from it and that he is safe from self-admiration. It is reported from some of the imams: praise does not harm one who knows himself. The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "I am the master of the sons of Adam and I say so without boasting," and the report is in full length.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 56:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Thus did We establish⁠﻿ ...﴾ It is narrated that the king appointed him to what he requested after a year, and he was brought forth wearing a crown set with jewels, and he seated him on a throne of gold, and he withdrew from the affair entirely and entrusted it to him, and the kings submitted to him, and he was called al-'Aziz. And in the story also: the wife of al-'Aziz, her husband died, and the king married her to Yusuf, peace be upon him, and she bore him two sons. And in some narrations: she stood on the road of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and called out: "Glory be to Him who made kings slaves through their disobedience, and made slaves kings through their obedience."

The words of the Most High: ﴿[We established]﴾ and its meaning is: We gave power and extended authority, ﴿to Yusuf in the land﴾, meaning: the land of Egypt, ﴿to settle therein wherever he willed﴾, meaning: he would dwell therein wherever he willed. ﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾, its meaning is: ﴿We bestow Our blessing upon whom We will﴾ ﴿and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾, the meaning is clear.

His saying: ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed﴾ means: the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed. And His saying: ﴿and they used to be mindful of God﴾ is clear in meaning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 58:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him﴾. The scholars of reports (ahl al-akhbar) said: When the king appointed Joseph, peace be upon him, to take charge of the affair and to manage the wealth of Egypt, he managed the gathering of food in the best manner. He built fortresses and great storehouses, gathered food in them for the years of drought, and spent from it in a reasonable way, until the years of abundance passed and the years of famine arrived. It is related that he used to set out the king's food and that of his household once a day, at midday. Whenever a year of famine came, the first to feel hunger was the king, who would call out at midnight: "O Joseph, hunger! Hunger!" In some reports it is said that he would allot food for two persons as food for two, and would place the whole of it before one person, who would eat only half of it. When the year of famine came, food for two was placed before one person, and he ate all of it and asked for more, so Joseph, peace be upon him, knew that the year of famine had arrived. And Allah knows best.

They said: The first year came with a terror and a severity such as people had never known, and every year that followed was more terrible and more severe. When the second year came, the famine reached Canaan, the dwelling of Jacob and his sons, and they were in great need of food. He called his sons and said to them: "I have heard that in Egypt there is a righteous king who sells food. Make ready and go to him to buy food from him." He sent them, and they were ten men, and he kept [his son Benjamin] with him. They arrived in Egypt. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿And the brothers of Joseph came﴾.

As for His words: ﴿and he recognised them﴾, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: he recognised them at the first glance at them. Al-Hasan said: he did not recognise them until they had made themselves known to him. The meaning of the verse: he recognised them with recognition. Ma'rifah (recognition) is the clarification of a thing in such a way that, if it were witnessed, one would distinguish it from anything else. His words: ﴿but they did not recognise him﴾ mean that they did not know him. Inkar (denial) is the nullification of knowledge by speech. If someone says: How did he recognise them while they did not [recognise him], although they were brothers?

The answer is in several respects. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: he wore the crown of the kingship and was seated on the royal throne, so they did not recognise him. Al-Kalbi mentioned that he was dressed in the fashion of the kings of Egypt and the non-Arabs.

The second view: he spoke to them from behind a screen, so they did not recognise him for this reason, while he recognised them because he saw them and they did not see him. This is the weakest of the views.

The third view: they had left him as a young boy, and between the time they sold him and the time they entered upon him there were forty years, so they did not recognise him for this reason. This is a good view. As for him, he had left them as men.

The fourth view: Joseph was expecting their arrival, so when they came he recognised them, whereas the brothers did not think that he would attain what he had attained, so they did not recognise him for this reason.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 59:

His words, ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾ to the end of the verse. Al-jihaz (the outfit) is the choicest of goods that is transported from one land to another. The meaning of tajhiz (furnishing) here is that he sold them the food, delivered it to them, and made it easy for them to return to their land.

And His words, ﴿He said, "Bring me a brother of yours from your father"﴾. In the narration: when they entered upon him, he took them aside in the house and said, "I have doubts about your condition, so tell me, who are you?" They said, "We are the sons of an upright man." He said, "And who is he?" They said, "Ya'qub (Jacob)." So he asked them about his state, and they mentioned that he had one other son, a full brother of theirs by the same mother, whom he kept for companionship. He said, "I have doubts about you. If you are truthful, then bring that brother with you, so that the doubt about your condition may be removed." It was also said: when the story was related to him, he said to them, "My story is like your story, O people. I lost a brother of mine from my mother, and I am greatly grieved over him, and his separation from me has embittered my kingship. So I wish that you would bring him to me, that I may complain to him of my sorrow and he may complain to me of his sorrow." It is by this means that he said, "Bring me a brother of yours from your father."

In some (tafsirs) it is mentioned that they described Ya'qub's preference of Binyamin (Benjamin) and his brother in love, so he wished to see Binyamin, to look whether he was the object of that preference.

And His words, ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure, and I am the best of hosts?﴾ meaning: I complete the measure and do not diminish it. And His words, ﴿and I am the best of hosts﴾: Mujahid said, "I am the best of those who host," and he had indeed honoured their hospitality well.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 60:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure [of grain] for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾ Al-Hasan said: "If you do not bring him to me, there will be no food for you with me if you come." And His saying: ﴿nor shall you come near me﴾ means: do not approach my land or my home.

The Exalted said: ﴿They said, "We will seek to persuade our father to let him go"﴾. Its meaning: we will ask his father to send him with us. And His words: ﴿"And indeed we will surely do it"﴾, meaning: we will exert ourselves.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 62:

His words: ﴿And he said to his servants﴾ It is recited in two readings: "li-fityānihi" and "li-fityatihi." The fatā (youth) is the young man complete in strength, while al-fityah and al-fityān here mean the boys. His words: ﴿Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags﴾. It is said that their merchandise was the money they had brought to buy food. It is related from some of them that their merchandise was eight skins of sawīq (a flour of parched grain) from al-muql (the doum palm). The sounder view is the first.

His words: ﴿into their saddlebags﴾. The rahl (saddlebag) here means the container for goods. It was also said: into their sacks (jawāliq).

His words: ﴿So that they may recognise it when they return to their family, so that perhaps they will come back﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: "So that perhaps they will recognise our generosity towards them and our kindness to them, and that will move them to return."

The second opinion: "So that they may recognise it (i.e., the merchandise) when they return to their family, and so return to give back the merchandise, to remove any suspicion of error."

Opinions differ as to why he returned their merchandise to them.

One of the opinions is what we have explained, namely that it was an incitement to them to return. The second: he knew that the dirhams were scarce with them, so he returned the dirhams to them to be a help to them in buying food. The third: he was ashamed to give his father and brothers the grain in exchange for the price, given their great need and his own abundance.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 63:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So when they returned to their father, they said: "O our father, measure has been withheld from us, so send our brother with us that we may obtain measure."﴾ That is, if we do not take our brother with us. The second view: he had given to each one of them a load in their names, but he had not given anything in the name of Benjamin, and he said: "Load him up, so that I may give in his name." This is the meaning of His words: ﴿measure has been withheld from us﴾, that is, measure has been withheld from us for Benjamin. By "measure" (al-kayl) is meant food, because it is measured out (yukal). His words: ﴿so send our brother with us that we may obtain measure﴾ mean: that we may measure out the food. It has also been said: that we may obtain measure for him. His words: ﴿And indeed we will be its guardians﴾ are clear.

**Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 12, verse 64:**

His saying, ﴿He said, "Shall I entrust him to you (هَل ءآمنكم عَلَيْهِ) as I entrusted his brother before?"﴾ the verse. The meaning of this is: how can I entrust him to you when you have done to Joseph what you have done?

His saying, ﴿But God is the best guardian﴾ is recited as "ḥifẓan" (حفظا) and "ḥāfiẓan" (حَافِظًا). Its meaning is: God's guarding is better than your guarding, and God's guardian is better than your guardian.

His saying, ﴿and He is the most merciful of the merciful﴾ is clear.

"The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when they opened their goods, they found their merchandise returned to them﴾, meaning: the dirhams they had carried. ﴿They said: O our father, what more could we want?﴾ In this there are two opinions. The first: "what (ma) do we seek?" as a question; this is the view of Qatadah. Its real meaning is that they mentioned to Ya'qub, peace be upon him, the king's kindness to them and his honouring of them, and they urged him by that to send Benjamin. Then, when they opened the goods and found the merchandise, they said: what more do we seek by way of words? This is the clear evidence of kindness and honour.

The second opinion: that "ma" here is for negation, and its meaning is: we do not seek from you any wealth with which to buy food. ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾: this money has been returned to us, so we will carry it and buy food with it. The first opinion is more sound.

As for His saying ﴿and we will get provisions for our family﴾: it is said "mara ahlahu" when he brings them food from one town to another; and al-mirah is the food carried. His saying ﴿and we will guard our brother﴾ means: from what you fear for him. His saying ﴿and gain an extra camel-load﴾: Mujahid said: "al-ba'ir" here means the donkey; he said: it is a dialect usage, and they were people of donkeys and had no camels. The more sound view is that it is the well-known camel. His saying ﴿and gain an extra camel-load﴾: they only said this because he was given one camel-load in the name of each man and no more; this is the meaning of His saying ﴿and gain an extra camel-load﴾. His saying ﴿That is an easy measure﴾ has two meanings: the first: that is a small measure, meaning what we have carried is small and does not suffice us and our family, so send our brother with us so that what we carry of food may increase. The second meaning: that is an easy measure, meaning easy for the one who measures it out."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 66:

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "I will never send him with you"﴾. In the narrative (al-qissa): the brothers suffered the utmost hardship, and the matter became straitened for Ya'qub (Ya'qub) and his people regarding food, so he had no choice but to send [Binyamin (Binyamin)] with them. He said: ﴿"I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn covenant (mawthiq) by Allah"﴾. The mawthiq is the covenant confirmed by an oath. It is also said: it is the covenant confirmed by calling Allah to witness against oneself. As for His words: ﴿"You must bring him back to me unless you are surrounded (by misfortune)"﴾, there are two views concerning it. The first: "unless you are all destroyed." The second: "unless a command comes to you from the heavens against which you have no power."

As for His words: ﴿So when they had given him their solemn covenant﴾, meaning: they gave it to him. ﴿He said, "Allah is Witness over what we say"﴾. Ya'qub said: "Allah is Witness over what we say." The wakil (wakil, trustee) is the one who takes charge of affairs. It is also said: wakil means witness (shahid) [and it is said: shahid, meaning witness]. It is also said: guardian (hafiz).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 67:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And he said, "O my sons, do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates."﴾ Most of the exegetes [hold] that he feared the evil eye (al-ʿayn), because they had been given beauty, strength and tall stature. This is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas and others among the exegetes; and the evil eye is real. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he would seek refuge for al-Hasan and al-Husayn, saying: "I seek refuge for you both in the perfect words of God from every devil and venomous creature, and from every envious eye that harms."

There are many reports on this subject, and in some transmitted reports: "The evil eye is real; it brings the camel to the cauldron and the man to the grave."

There is another opinion regarding the verse: that he feared the king of Egypt would, upon seeing their strength and unity, imprison them or kill them. It is related from Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi that he said: Yaʿqub was hoping that they would see Yusuf and find him, so he said: ﴿And enter from different gates﴾ so that perhaps you may find Yusuf [or] meet him. The sound opinion is the first.

As for His saying: ﴿And I cannot avail you anything against God; the decision belongs only to God﴾, its meaning is: if God has decreed a decree concerning you, it will befall you whether you are gathered or dispersed. The meaning of "ughni" (avail) is: to repel. In a report: "Caution does not avert destiny." As for His saying: ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾, this is Yaʿqub, peace be upon him, entrusting his affairs to God. And "hukm" (judgment) is: the separating between disputants according to human knowledge, and from God it is an act according to wisdom. ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾, meaning: in Him I have trusted and upon Him I have depended.

﴿And upon Him let those who rely [upon Him] rely﴾, meaning: in Him trust those who trust.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 68:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾ mean: from the separate gates. It has been said: the city was the city of al-Farama, and it had four gates; it was the city of al-'Arish. And His words ﴿It did not avail them against Allah in anything﴾ mean: it did not ward off from them anything from Allah. This truth is a confirmation of what Ya'qub (Jacob) said, namely His words: ﴿And I could not avail you against Allah in anything﴾. And His words: ﴿except a need in the soul of Ya'qub which he fulfilled﴾ mean: except a desire of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, which he mentioned, and the matter proceeded in accordance with that. And His words: ﴿And indeed, he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him﴾. The people of tafsir said: its meaning is that he acted by knowledge, not by ignorance. Some of them said: "And indeed, he was a possessor of knowledge because of Our teaching him." ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾, because they did not take the path of knowledge.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 69:

His saying: ﴿When they entered upon Yusuf, he drew his brother to himself﴾. "Drew to himself" (āwā ilayhi) means he joined him to himself, and its meaning is: he lodged him with himself. In the narrative it is related that he lodged every two brothers of the same mother together in a house, and Benjamin remained alone, so he said: "Stay with me." Each pair of brothers of the same mother had been [lodged] separately.

And his saying: ﴿He said: Indeed, I am your brother﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: that he secretly told him that he was his brother. The second: that he said: "I am in place of your brother who is lost." This was related by Wahb and others.

And his saying: ﴿So do not be distressed by what they used to do﴾. Its meaning: do not grieve over what they did to your brother, for I am a replacement for your brother. It is related that Benjamin said to him: "And who would find a brother like you, O king? But you are not from Ya'qub." Then at that point he mentioned that he was truly his brother.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 70:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When he had furnished them with their provisions﴾ — we have already mentioned it. And His saying: ﴿and he put the drinking-cup﴾ — the saqayah (drinking-cup) is the vessel from which one drinks. They differed as to what it was made of. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was of chrysolite (zabarjad). Mujahid said: it was of silver, inlaid with jewels. It was also said: it was of gold. And it is reported from some of them: that it was an elongated vessel, resembling a measuring bowl (mukkuk), having two heads, with a handle in its middle. So it would be measured out from one of the two heads and drunk from the other head. It was not used for measuring except with it, because of the scarcity of food. And a sound would be heard from it: "It has been measured out for such-and-such."

His saying: ﴿in his brother's bag﴾ — that is, in the bag of his brother, among his provisions. And His saying: ﴿Then a caller called out﴾ — it is related that he left them until they had gone a stage, and it was said: until they had gone out into the open country and departed from the settlement. Then he sent someone after them who stopped them and said: ﴿O caravan, you are indeed thieves.﴾ The ʿir (caravan) are the owners of the donkeys, and it was also said that the word may be used to mean the camels.

If someone says: How did Yusuf permit himself to accuse them of theft when they had not stolen?

The answer to this is in several respects. The first: its meaning is: you are indeed thieves of Yusuf from his father, and you acted as thieves act. The second: the man said it without Yusuf's order, for when the cup was missing he thought they had stolen it. The third: this was a lapse on the part of Yusuf, peace be upon him. And they have said: he committed three lapses. The first: when he intended (sin) with the wife of al-ʿAziz until he saw the proof. The second: when he said to the cupbearer: "Mention me to your lord." The third: this, namely that he attributed his brothers to theft.

The first opinion is the best of the opinions. It is said that he had agreed a signal with Benjamin, and that he said what he said by prior arrangement. And God knows best.

The Qur'anic quotation ﴿قَالُوا وَأَقْبلُوا عَلَيْهِم مَاذَا تَفْقِدُونَ﴾ is translated as: "They said, turning towards them: 'What is it that you are missing?'"

His saying (the Exalted): "They said, turning towards them: 'What is it that you are missing?'" It is related that they halted and said to the people: "What are you looking for?"

"They said, 'We have lost the king's goblet.'" Yahya ibn Ya'mar read it as "ṣawgh al-malik" with the letter ghayn, and ṣawgh means gold or silver (a goblet or vessel of gold or silver). The word ṣwāʿ (the measuring vessel/drinking cup) may be masculine or feminine, and ṣwāʿ is the drinking vessel (al-siqāya) mentioned in the first verse. It is also said that it used to be placed before the king, and when it was needed it was taken.

Regarding His words, ﴿and for him who brings it there is a camel-load﴾, meaning: and for whoever returns it, there is a camel-load of food.

Regarding His words, ﴿and I am its guarantor﴾, meaning: I am its surety. Za'īm, kafīl and ḍamīn (guarantor, surety) have the same meaning, and a leader is called za'īm because he takes charge of the affairs of the people and speaks on their behalf. If it is asked: Is a surety for an unknown thing valid according to you, and is this a surety for an unknown thing? We say: it is not valid. It is possible that the camel-load was of known measure among them. Second: this is a ju'āla (a reward offered for a specified act), not a kafāla (a surety), and according to us such a ju'āla is valid.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 73:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They said, "By Allah, you know well that we did not come to cause corruption in the land."﴾ Meaning: "By Allah, we did not come to cause corruption in the land," that is, "to steal in the kingdom of Egypt." ﴿And we were not thieves.﴾ In our own land, we would not steal and then steal in your land.

If someone says: How did they say, "You know well," when their answer should have been, "We do not know"? We say: They said that because they were a group that had strength and power, and they did not wrong anyone on the road, nor did they let their animals enter anyone's field to graze. It is reported that when they entered Egypt, they placed the saddlebags over the heads of their animals so that they would not damage anything.

Another answer: They only said this because they returned the merchandise that was carried in their saddlebags. They said: "If we were thieves, we would not have returned the merchandise, for whoever wants to steal something does not let go of anything that falls into his hand."

If it is asked: How is it permissible in Arabic for a speaker to say "Ta-llahi" (by Allah), but not to say "Ta-r-Rahman" or "Ta-r-Rahim"? We say: Because the "ta" (ت) is a replacement for the "ba" (ب), since the original form of the oath is the particle "ba." Then the "waw" (و) was replaced by the "ta" (ت). When it was a substitute of a substitute, it became weakened in its usage and was restricted to the noun that is the original form of the oath by custom and by language, which is "Allah."
The Exalted's words: ﴿They said, "What then will be its requital if you are liars?"﴾ Its meaning: "What then is the requital of the thief, if you are lying in your statement that we did not steal?"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 75:

His saying: ﴿They said: "The recompense for it is: he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself is its recompense."﴾ The enslaving of the thief who is found in whose saddlebag [this] is its recompense, so that the second clause is an emphasis of the first. In the first there is an ellipsis, in keeping with the habit of Arabic speech. The second opinion: they said, "Its recompense is: he in whose saddlebag it is found; so the thief is its recompense." Thus it is a metonymy for the thief, and the meaning of making it (the recompense) is that he is to be enslaved and kept in bondage. Know that it was the custom of Ya'qub (Jacob) that whoever stole something would be enslaved for a year. The ruling of the king of Egypt was that the thief be beaten and made to pay twice the value of the item. So Yusuf's aim was to detain his brother with him, and he returned the ruling on theft to them. They mentioned a ruling on theft from what they knew of the law of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, so Yusuf, peace be upon him, acted upon that, and his aim of detaining his brother was achieved.

As for His saying: ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾ It means: the brothers of Yusuf said, "Thus do we recompense thieves among us."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 76:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother, then brought it out from his brother's bag.﴾ It is related that the crier searched their bags, and it is related that he (Yusuf) had them brought back to Yusuf, peace be upon him, and he ordered their bags to be searched in front of him. In the narrative: that man would, each time he searched a bag and did not find the drinking bowl (al-sa'), seek forgiveness from God and show repentance. When only Benjamin's baggage remained, he said: "I do not think this one has taken anything." They said: "By God, we will not leave you until you search his bag, so that our hearts and yours are at ease." He searched his bag and brought out the drinking bowl. They remained crushed and ashamed, and they lowered their heads in embarrassment, and they said to Benjamin: "What is this, son of Rachel?" ﴿He said: "By God, I did not steal." They said: "How, when the bowl has been found in your baggage?"﴾ He said: "The bowl was placed in my baggage by the one who placed the merchandise in your baggage." He said: "They seized Benjamin as a slave (raqiq), a servant (abd)." In the narrative: that man seized him by the neck and returned him to Yusuf, as thieves are returned. As for His saying: ﴿Thus did We plan for Yusuf.﴾ Its meaning: We devised for Yusuf. It was also said: We contrived for Yusuf. Ibn al-Anbari said: We intended for Yusuf; and he recited the verse of the poet:

(Kādat wa-kidtu wa-dhāka khayru irāda ... law ʿāda min lahw al-ṣabāba mā maḍā)

If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying "thus" (kadhalika), and what is this kaf, when the kaf denotes comparison? The answer: this refers to the saying of Yaqub at the beginning of the surah: ﴿Lest they plot against you a plot.﴾ Their plot was that they took him from his father by a stratagem and cast him into the well. God, exalted is He, said: as they plotted concerning the matter of Yusuf, ﴿We plotted for Yusuf﴾ concerning their affair. Plotting (kayd) from creatures is stratagem (ḥīla), and from God it is planning (tadbīr) with truth. His saying: ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law.﴾ Its meaning: Yusuf could not have requited his brother under the king's judgment. It was also said: under the king's custom. The poet said:

(Aqūlu wa-qad daraʾtu lahā wadīnī ... ahādhā dīnuhu abadan wa-dīnī)

Here "mā" is for negation. His saying: ﴿Except that God wills.﴾ Its meaning: except by the will of God, i.e., he did what he did by the will of God, exalted is He. His saying: ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will.﴾ He said this in this place, because He raised Yusuf's degree above theirs in knowledge, kingship, intellect and other things. It was also said: We raise in degrees whom We will through success and protection. His saying: ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: and above every scholar is a scholar, until knowledge ends with God. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "and above every scholar is one who knows (ʿalīm)."

"Qur'anic quotation: ﴿They said: If he steals, then indeed a brother of his stole before.﴾ They meant by his brother from before: Yusuf, peace be upon him. And there has been disagreement about what it was that he (Yusuf) stole."

Careful: the source text uses "أيش" which is colloquial; render it as "what" in English. Let me write the full translation properly.

**Translation:**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They said: If he steals, then indeed a brother of his stole before.﴾ They meant by his brother from before: Yusuf, peace be upon him. And there has been disagreement over what it was that he stole.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: He had with his paternal grandfather's (mother's side) an image that was worshipped, so he took it secretly and threw it away, lest it be worshipped. The second view: he used to take food from his father's table secretly and give it to the poor.

The third view: he was with his paternal aunt, who was raising him, and Ya'qub wanted to take him away from her. So his aunt tied a belt (mintaqah) under his garments and claimed that he had stolen it, in order to keep him with herself and leave him with her, for she disliked that he be taken from her, and she loved him very intensely. This was related by Ibn Ishaq.

And His words: ﴿So Yusuf kept it hidden within himself﴾. If someone says: To what does the statement ﴿So Yusuf kept it hidden within himself and did not reveal it to them﴾ refer? We say: there is no previous mention of this, and its meaning is: he kept the statement hidden within himself, and that statement was his saying: ﴿You are worse in position﴾, and he did not declare this statement openly. And His words: ﴿worse in position﴾ mean: worse in conduct. The reality of its meaning is that there was no true theft from Yusuf, whereas there was a true theft from you; that is your stealing of Yusuf from his father.

And His words: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of what you describe﴾ mean: Allah knows best whether his brother stole or did not steal.

They said: "O Chief (al-'Aziz), indeed he has an aged father, so take one of us in his place. Indeed we see you to be among the good-doers." (Qur'an 12:78)

Regarding the narrative: they became extremely angry at this situation. Yahudha (Judah) was such that when he became angry, nothing could withstand his anger, and when he shouted, every pregnant woman who heard his shout would miscarry her child. Yet, despite this, if any of the sons of Ya'qub (Jacob) touched him, his anger would subside. It is also said that this was the characteristic of Shim'un (Simeon), one of the sons of Ya'qub. It is narrated that he said to his brothers: "How many markets are there in Egypt?" They said: "Ten markets." He said: "You take care of the markets, and I will take care of the kingship," or he said: "You take care of the kingship, and I will take care of the markets." They said: Then they entered upon Yusuf, and Yahudha said to him: "Will you return our brother to us, or I will shout a shout that will cause every pregnant woman in this city to miscarry her child." Yusuf had a young son standing beside him, and he said: "Go, take the hand of that man and bring him to me." So he went, took his hand, and his anger subsided. Then he said to his brothers: "By God, there is among us a seed of the seed of Ya'qub." The young son said to him: "And who is Ya'qub? I do not know Ya'qub or his offspring." It is also narrated that he became angry a second time, so Yusuf rose to him, kicked him with his leg, and seized him by his collar, so that he fell to the ground, and said: "O company of the Hebrews, do you think there is no one stronger than you?" As-Suddi and others related all of this. When their affair reached this point, they humbled themselves and became submissive, and they said: "O Chief, indeed he has an aged father, so take one of us in his place."

Al-'Izz (might/honour): the prevention of oppression or harm through abundance of authority and power. Al-'Aziz is the one who is unassailable because of the vast power that he possesses.

His saying: "Indeed he has an aged father, so take one of us in his place," means: take one of us in his stead. The word shaykhan is in the accusative as a qualifier of "aban."

His saying: "Indeed we see you to be among the good-doers" means: indeed we see you to be among those who do good to us. His goodness toward them was in fulfilling the measure, in good hospitality, in returning their merchandise, and other things.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 79:

The words of the Most High: ﴿He said, "We seek refuge in Allah"﴾ meaning, "I seek protection in Allah" ﴿that we should take anyone except him with whom we found our property; indeed, we would then be wrongdoers﴾. Its meaning is clear, and its meaning is: that we should take the innocent in place of the one who committed the crime. So if we were to take him, we would then be wrongdoers.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 80:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When they despaired of him﴾. Regarding the story: when the cup was taken out and the brothers returned to him, he called for the cup and struck it with a rod in his hand, and the cup spoke.

﴿The eldest of them said: "Did you not know that your father had taken a solemn pledge from you in God's name, and that before this you had failed in regard to Joseph? So I will not leave this land until my father gives me leave, or God decides for me; and He is the best of judges."﴾

He said: "O people, this cup is indeed telling me a report." They said: "And what does it tell you, O king?" He said: "It tells me that you were (eleven) brothers, that you took a brother of yours from your father, threw him into the well, and afterwards sold him." He said: Then they looked at one another, and Binyamin stood up and prostrated to him, and said: "Your cup has spoken the truth, O king. Ask it: is my brother alive or not?" So he struck the cup a second time, and it spoke, and he said: "It says: he is alive, and you will see him." He said: "Ask it who stole the cup?" He said: "It is angry, meaning the cup, and says: how do you ask me, when you saw it in the hand of the one you were with?!" Narrated by al-Naqqash, Abu al-Hasan ibn Faris and others. And God knows best.

As for His saying: ﴿When they despaired of him﴾, meaning: they gave up hope of him. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Istay'asu" means they became certain that the brother would not be returned to them. He recited:

(I say to them in al-Shi'b when they capture me... Did you not know that I am the son of Faris Zahdam?)

Meaning: "Did you not know?" As for His saying ﴿They withdrew apart, conferring privately﴾, meaning: they went off alone, conferring and consulting regarding the matter of their brother. The meaning of ﴿khalasu﴾ is that no one else was with them. The Arabs say: "qawm najiy" (a people in private conference). The poet said:

(Until, when the people were in private conference, and their affairs were mixed up like ropes.)

As for His saying ﴿The eldest of them said﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: he is Yahudha (Judah), and he was not the oldest of them in age, but he was the oldest in intellect. Mujahid said: he is Shim'un (Simeon), and leadership over his brothers belonged to him. Qatada said: he is Ruben (Reuben), and he was the oldest of them in age.

As for His saying: ﴿Did you not know that your father had taken a solemn pledge from you in God's name﴾: we have already explained the meaning of "mawthiq" (solemn pledge). As for His saying ﴿and that before this you had failed in regard to Joseph﴾, meaning: you were negligent and abandoned your father's covenant.

As for His saying ﴿So I will not leave this land﴾, meaning: I will not leave the land of Egypt ﴿until my father gives me leave﴾, meaning: my father calls me back ﴿or God decides for me﴾, meaning: returns my brother to me. It was also said: God decides for me by the sword, so that I fight them and recover my brother. ﴿And He is the best of judges﴾, meaning: He is the best of those who decide.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 81:

The Most High's saying: ﴿Return to your father﴾ and the verse [continues]: Go to your father. ﴿And say: O our father, indeed your son has stolen﴾. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited: "innahu in ibnaka saraqa" (that he, indeed, your son has stolen). In it there are two meanings: one of them: he was accused of theft. The other: theft was known from him. As for His saying: ﴿And we did not testify except to what we knew﴾, it means: except to what we saw, for we saw the taking out of the measuring cup from his baggage. As for His saying: ﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen﴾, in it there are two opinions: one of them: we were not guardians of his night and day, nor of his departure and his coming, and we only knew of his condition while he was with us. The second opinion, meaning: that if we had known that he would steal, we would not have carried him with ourselves; but we did not know this unseen matter.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 82:

The Exalted One said: ﴿And ask the town in which we were﴾, meaning: the people of the town in which we were. ﴿And the caravan in which we came﴾, meaning: and the people of the caravan in which we came, i.e., we were in it.

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾, it is obvious. If someone says: How could Yusuf (peace be upon him) permit himself to do all of this to his father, without informing him of his whereabouts, without sending anyone to him, and then detaining his brother with him, though he knew how intense his father's grief over him was? This is greater than any disobedience, and it involves severing the ties of kinship and a lack of compassion. The answer to this: People have said much about this, and the correct view is that he did what he did by the command of God, the Exalted, and God commanded him to do so in order to increase Ya'qub's trial and multiply his reward, and to raise his rank [so that he would join] in rank his forefathers who had passed away. It has also been said that he did not reveal himself to the brothers, because he did not feel safe from them scheming against him and concealing it from their father. The correct view is the first.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 83:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you."﴾ In the verse there is an abridgment, for they returned and related to their father what their eldest had told them, and then Ya'qub said what he said. The meaning of taswil (beautifying, making seem fair) here is: your souls adorned for you the bringing of your brother to Egypt, so that you might seek a quick benefit.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So patience is becoming.﴾ That is: my patience is beautiful patience. Sabr (patience) is restraining the soul from what it longs for, and we have already explained the meaning of jamil (beautiful). And His saying: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me.﴾ That is: Yusuf, his brother Binyamin, and Yahudha. In the narration: the Angel of Death, peace be upon him, visited Ya'qub and said to him: "O king, good of scent, handsome of form, have you taken the soul of your son among the spirits?" He said: "No." So Ya'qub was calmed by this, knew that he was alive, and hoped to see him. And His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.﴾ Its meaning: All-Knowing of their whereabouts, All-Wise in their management.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 84:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And he turned away from them and said, "Oh, my grief over Joseph!"﴾ — the verse. It is related that when Benjamin was detained by Joseph, the matter weighed heavily upon Ya'qub (Jacob) to the utmost degree of severity, his sorrow reached its limit, and he could no longer restrain his patience, so he wailed. This is the meaning of His words ﴿and he turned away from them﴾, i.e., he turned away from them, ﴿and said, "Oh, my grief!"﴾.

Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Some of Ya'qub's brothers visited him and said to him, 'O Ya'qub, what has blinded your eyes and bent your back?' He said, 'My eyes were blinded by much weeping over Joseph, and my back was bent by the intensity of grief over Benjamin.' So Allah, may He be exalted, sent Jibril (peace be upon him) to him, and said, 'O Ya'qub, do you complain of Me to My creation?' After that he entered his house and shut its door, and ﴿said, 'I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah'﴾."

The meaning of His words ﴿Oh, my grief!﴾ is: O grief over Joseph! And al-asaf (grief) means intense sorrow.

His words ﴿and his eyes turned white from the grief﴾ mean: whiteness overcame the pupil and sight was lost. He attributed it to grief because he wept from intense sorrow and became blind from excessive weeping.

His words ﴿so he was suppressing (his grief)﴾ mean: he kept his grief restrained, not disclosing it or mentioning it to people. This is after Allah had forbidden him from that, as we have explained.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 85:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph"﴾, meaning: you will not cease remembering Joseph, and the "not" (lā) is elided. And His saying: ﴿until you become consumed by grief﴾. Tha'lab, Ahmad ibn Yahya, said: ḥarḍ (consumed, wasted) is everything that is of no benefit. Mujahid said: ḥarḍ is what falls short of death. Al-Farra' said: ḥarḍ is the one whose body and intellect have deteriorated. Abu 'Ubayda said: ḥarḍ is the one whom grief has melted away. It has also been said: it is one whose condition has become wasted and whose health is ruined. The sayings are close in meaning.

It is narrated from Anas ibn Malik that he recited: "ḥattā takūna ḥarḍan" (until you become a ḥarḍ). And ḥarḍ is the ashnān (a plant used for washing, i.e., soapwort or the like), and its meaning is: until you become like the stick of the ashnān [that has been worn away]. And His saying: ﴿or you become among those who perish﴾, meaning: among the dead.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 12, verse 86:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know."﴾ We have already set out the report transmitted on this matter through the narration of Anas. Al-bath (البث) means sorrow (al-hamm), ﴿and my grief to Allah﴾. It is related that he said: "O Lord, will You not have mercy on me? You have taken from me such-and-such" – and he began enumerating – "return to me my darling (rayhanati), so that I may smell her, and then do with me what You will, and I shall not mind." Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed to him: "Be still and calm your heart, for I shall return them both to you."

In the established reports transmitted from al-Hasan al-Basri, he said: "Ya'qub wept for eighty years, and his tear never dried up, and there was no one on the face of the earth more honoured by Allah than him."

His saying: ﴿and I know from Allah what you do not know﴾ means: I know from the life of Yusuf what you do not know. It was also said: I know from the fulfilment of Yusuf's dream what you do not know.

If someone says: How did Ya'qub weep all this weeping and grieve this grief? Was he afflicted with anything more than the loss of one son? Should he not have committed the matter to Allah, may He be exalted, and been patient? The answer to this is: he was tested in this with what no one else had been tested with. He did not ask about Yusuf despite the long passage of time, and his trial was that he did not know whether Yusuf was alive, so that he might hope to see him, nor did he know that he had died, so that he might stop asking about him. Yusuf, among all the brothers, had been singled out with complete beauty, (and intellect), good character, and all that inclines the heart towards him.

It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that when his brother died he wept for him intensely, and he was asked about that, and he said: "Glory be to the One who has not made grief a shame for its people," and he recited His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾.

Habib ibn Abi Thabit reported: When Ya'qub grew old and grief lasted long upon him, his eyebrows fell over his eyes from old age, so he would lift them with a cloth. Some of his neighbours entered upon him and said: "What has brought you to this state, when you have not yet reached your father's age?" He said: "The long passage of time and the abundance of sorrows." So Allah sent Jibril, upon him be peace, to him and said: "O Ya'qub, have you complained of Me to My creation?" He said: "A sin – so forgive it for me, O Lord." Allah forgave it for him, and after that, whenever he was asked about his condition, he would say: "Indeed, I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah."

It is related from Wahb ibn Munabbih that Allah, may He be exalted, revealed to Ya'qub, upon him be peace: "Do you know why I punished you and separated you from your son?" He said: "No, O Lord." He said: "Because you slaughtered a sheep, roasted it, and withheld from your neighbour, and ate and did not feed him."

Anas has also transmitted something close to this from the Prophet, which al-Hakim Abu 'Abd Allah has cited. In the report of Anas: "Allah, may He be exalted, said to Ya'qub: Prepare a meal and invite the poor to it. He did so, and after that, whenever he had his morning meal, he would order someone to call out: 'Whoever wishes to eat lunch, let him come to Ya'qub'; and whenever he broke his fast, he would order someone to call out: 'Whoever wishes to break his fast, let him come to Ya'qub.' So a large group would eat their midday meal with him, and a large group of the poor would have their evening meal with him."

In the story it is said that the cause of Ya'qub's trial was that he slaughtered a calf in front of its mother while she was lowing.

It is related from Abd Allah ibn Yazid and Ibn Abi Farwa that Ya'qub, upon him be peace, wrote a letter to Yusuf when Benjamin was detained: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. From Ya'qub, Israel of Allah, son of Ishaq, the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Ibrahim, the friend of Allah, to the king of Egypt. To proceed: we are a household upon whom trials have been heaped. As for my grandfather Ibrahim, his hands and feet were bound and he was thrown into the fire, but Allah made it cool and safe for him. As for my father Ishaq, his hands and feet were bound and the knife was placed upon his throat, but Allah ransomed him with a ram. As for me, I was tested with separation from the dearest of my children to me, and I used to console myself with his brother from his mother. You have detained him and claimed that he stole. By Allah, I am not a thief, and I have not begotten a thief. If you return him to me, well and good; otherwise I shall invoke upon you a supplication that will overtake the seventh of your offspring." When the letter reached him, he wept intensely and revealed himself to what was due to be shown.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 87:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O my sons, go and search for Joseph and his brother﴾. Al-tahassus (searching by means of the senses): seeking a thing through the senses. Its meaning: seek and investigate for news of Joseph and his brother.

And His saying: ﴿And do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾. In the irregular (shadh) readings it was recited: "min rawh Allah" (and it is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he recited: "min rahmat Allah"). Rawh is derived from rih (wind), and in reality it is that by which one finds rest. It has also been said: "from the rawh of Allah," meaning: from the relief (faraj) of Allah, as said by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. It has also been said: from the mercy of Allah, and it has been said: from the bounty of Allah.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the rawh of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾. The meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 88:

His saying, exalted is He: (﴿Then when they entered upon him﴾ they said, "O 'Azeez (ruler), adversity has touched us and our family.") That is: hunger and need. And His saying: ﴿And we have come with poor merchandise﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: their dirhams were debased (zuyuf) in this year, and they were not accepted for food; this is the meaning of muzjah (poor, insufficient). From Mujahid and Qatadah: muzjah means few and meagre. Muqatil said: their merchandise was the green berry (habbat al-Khadra'). From al-Kalbi who said: their merchandise was ropes and the making of sacks. It was also said: it was the flour of muqul (a kind of fruit).

Ka'b said: it was ten dinars. It was also said: the goods of the Bedouins were wool, dried curd (aqit) and other things. His saying: ﴿So give us full measure﴾ means: complete it, as you used to complete it every time. His saying: ﴿and be charitable to us﴾ means: with what lies between the sound and the defective (currency). It was also said: be charitable to us by overlooking (our shortfall). The poet said:

(Be charitable to us, O son of 'Affan, and seek your reward... and appoint over us al-Ash'ari for nights.)

They meant Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. It was also said: and be charitable to us by releasing our brother. From Mujahid, who said: it is disliked for a man to say, "O Allah, be charitable to me," because charity is only from one who seeks reward. If someone says: how did they say "and be charitable to us" when charity is not lawful for the prophets? The answer: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: it was lawful for them. Moreover, we have explained that what is meant is overlooking and leniency, and this is permissible by consensus. His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable﴾: they did not say "He will reward you," because they did not trust his faith, so they said "Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable" in general terms for this purpose.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 89:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother, when you were ignorant?"﴾ It is narrated that when they said this, and Joseph heard it, compassion overcame him, and he said to them this statement: "Do you know what you did", meaning: what you did to Joseph and his brother. What they did to his brother was separating him from them, and he did not mention what they did to Ya'qub (Jacob), out of consideration for his dignity and in honour of him. As for His saying: ﴿when you were ignorant﴾, its meaning is: when you were sinful and disobedient. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "when you were children," and from al-Hasan that he said: "when you were young men, and with you was the ignorance of young men." In the story: when he said this statement, he smiled, and they saw his front teeth arranged like pearls, so they recognised him and said:

They said, "Are you indeed Joseph?" Some scholars said: they said this out of supposition (tawahhum), and they had not yet become certain until he said to them, "I am Joseph." As for His words, ﴿I am Joseph, and this is my brother﴾, al-Dahhak related that in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "and this is my brother, between him and me is kinship (qurba)." As for His words, ﴿Allah has been gracious to us﴾, meaning: Allah has bestowed His favour upon us. ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient, then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾: its meaning is, whoever refrains from sins (yattaqi 'an al-ma'asi) and is patient in acts of obedience and in calamities. It is related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he said: "Whoever refrains from fornication (al-zina) and is patient in celibacy (al-'uzuba)."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 91:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: "By God, God has certainly preferred you over us, and we were indeed sinners."﴾ That is, God has favoured you over us. ﴿And we were indeed sinners﴾, meaning: "We were nothing but sinners." It is also said: "We had indeed been sinners." The difference between khata' (خطأ) and akhta' (أَخْطَأ) is that khata' means to sin deliberately, while akhta' means to err without intending it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 92:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "No reproach will there be upon you today."﴾ At-tathrib (reproach) is reproach, as mentioned by Tha'lab and others. It was also said: "No reproach upon you today" means: there is no punishment upon you today after your admission of the sin. The poet said:

(So I pardoned you with a pardon free of reproach... and left you to a punishment of an everlasting day.)

As for His saying: ﴿Today Allah will forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾, its meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Go with this shirt of mine﴾. It is related that when God, exalted is He, made the fire cool and safe (bardan wa salaman) for Ibrahim, He sent down to him a shirt of silk from Paradise. Ibrahim gave it to Ishaq, and Ishaq gave it to Ya'qub. Ya'qub placed it in a (qasaba) [a small case or tube], sealed its head, and hung it around the neck of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and it remained on his neck. When this time came, God sent Jibril, peace be upon him, saying: "Open the case, and send the shirt to him, for no afflicted person touches it except that he is healed, and no sick person except that he recovers and is cured." So that shirt was sent to Ya'qub. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Go with this shirt of mine﴾. In the story, Yahudha said: "I will take the shirt to him, for I once took the shirt to him stained with blood." So he gave it to him, and he went out barefoot [bareheaded] running, with seven loaves of bread with him, and he did not finish them until he reached Kan'an. It was also said that it was sent by the hand of someone else. And [He said]: ﴿Cast it over the face of my father, and he will come back seeing﴾. Al-Farra' said: he will return seeing. Others said: he will return to sight. Al-Hasan said: he did not know that he would return seeing except after God informed him of that.

And His saying: ﴿And bring me all your family﴾, i.e., bring me all your family.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 94:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the caravan departed﴾ means: it separated from Egypt and set out. His saying: ﴿Their father said, "Indeed, I detect the scent of Joseph"﴾. In the narrative it is related that the east wind (rīḥ al-Ṣabā) asked its Lord permission to bring the scent of Joseph to Jacob, peace be upon them both, and it was the one that brought the scent of Joseph. Al-Ṣabā is a wind that comes from the direction of the east; when it blows upon the bodies it brings softness, comfort and pleasantness, and it stirs longing for loved ones and yearning for homelands. The poet said:

(O two hills of Na'mān, by God, leave the path of al-Ṣabā open to reach its breeze,)

(for indeed al-Ṣabā is a wind that, when it breathes upon a grieving heart, its cares are relieved.)

It is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "I was given victory by al-Ṣabā, and 'Ād was destroyed by al-Dabūr." It is also related that when the shirt was spread out, the scent of Paradise wafted from it, and Jacob, peace be upon him, smelled it and knew that it came from the shirt of Joseph, because there was nothing of Paradise on earth other than it.

His saying: ﴿Unless you think me senile﴾ means: unless you consider my judgment weak. It is also said: unless you call me foolish. And it is said: unless you attribute to me fear and ignorance.

The poet said:

(O my two companions, leave off blame and stop, for love has lasted long and you have prolonged the reproach.)

"The Exalted's saying: ﴿They said, 'By God, you are surely in your old error.'﴾ This is the statement of the sons of his sons, for his sons were in Egypt. Its meaning: 'By God, you are surely in your old mistake.' And error (khata') is departing from the path of what is right. For they held that Yusuf had died, and they saw that Ya'qub had become fixated on mentioning him, for he would come out of his house and a man would meet him carrying something, and he would say, 'Put it down and listen to my account.' And a servant-girl would meet him and he would say to her the same kind of thing. They thought him senile and greatly mistaken. This is the meaning of their saying, 'You are surely in your old error.' It has also been said: 'You are surely in your [misery] of old,' where shaqa' (misery) here means hardship (ta'ab). It has also been said: 'in your old heedlessness'; and it has been said: 'in your old love.' Al-Hasan al-Basri said: 'This was a great (ʿazim) disobedience (ʿuquq) on their part.'"

"The Almighty's saying: ﴿So when the bearer of good news came, he cast it over his face﴾ — its meaning: he cast the shirt over his face. And His saying: ﴿and he regained his sight﴾ — that is, he returned to sight and came back seeing. It is related that his strength returned at once, the film (al-ghishawa) was removed, and the whiteness that had been in his eye disappeared, and he opened his eyes in the finest state. And ﴿he said﴾ to his sons and his grandsons: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know from God what you do not know?﴾ This is evidence that he had told them: 'Yusuf is alive, and I hope to see him.' (And it was said): ﴿I know from God what you do not know﴾ means: from the realisation of Yusuf's dream, what you do not know. In some reports it is said that he said to the bearer of good news: 'I have nothing to give you, but may God make the agonies of death easy for you.' And it is related that when the news of Yusuf reached him, he asked the bearer of good news: 'On what religion did you leave Yusuf?' He said: 'On the religion of Islam.' He said: 'Now the blessing is complete.'"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins. Indeed, we were sinners."﴾ This is evidence that they had done what they did while they were adult, having reached puberty (bāligh).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 12, verse 98:

On His saying, ﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you"﴾. It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) and a group of the Tabi'un (Successors) that they said: "He delayed the supplication until the time of sahar (the last part of the night), which is the time when Allah, the Exalted, says: 'Is there anyone calling upon Me, that He may be answered? Is there anyone asking, that he may be given what he asks?' (the report) 'Is there anyone seeking forgiveness, that He may forgive him?'"

The second view is that he delayed it until the night of Friday. This is related from Ibn Abbas, and it has been narrated in some reports traced directly to the Prophet (ﷺ).

It is also related from Ata' ibn Maysara al-Khurasani that he said: "The need directed to the young is answered more quickly than the need directed to the elders. Indeed, Yusuf (peace be upon him) said: ﴿No reproach will be upon you today; may Allah forgive you﴾, and he did not delay, whereas when they asked Ya'qub, he said 'soon' and delayed."

In the story it is also mentioned that Ya'qub used to pray at night, and Yusuf would stand behind him, and his sons would stand behind Yusuf and ask forgiveness for them, in this manner for twenty years, until the revelation came down with their forgiveness.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾, its meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 99:

The Exalted's saying, ﴿So when they entered upon Yusuf, he drew his parents close to him﴾. It is narrated that Yusuf sent two hundred riding beasts and abundant provisions so that they might come to Ya'qub and his people. Masruq said: "They were ninety-three, between men and women." It is also narrated: "Seventy-two," and this is the more well-known. The people of reports (ahl al-akhbar) said: When Musa departed with the Children of Israel from Egypt, their number had reached six hundred thousand fighting men and seventy thousand, and the offspring were one million and seven hundred thousand. Likewise, in the story, they came, and when they drew near to Egypt, ﴿and he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration. And he said, "O my father, this is the interpretation of my vision from before."﴾ Yusuf went out to meet them with the army. It is also narrated that he carried the great king (al-malik al-akbar) along with himself. When they reached Ya'qub, they said to Ya'qub: "This is your son, who has come." He said: Yusuf wanted to greet him first with peace, but Jibril said: "No, until Ya'qub begins with the greeting of peace." So (Ya'qub) said: "Peace be upon you, O remover of sorrows (madhhab al-ahzan)." It is also narrated that the two of them dismounted and embraced. In some narratives, they walked, and Yusuf went ahead by a step, so Jibril came and said to him: "Will you go ahead of your father? No prophet will ever come forth from your progeny." In some narratives: Yusuf was with four thousand soldiers, and it has been said otherwise.

As for His saying, ﴿he drew his parents close to him﴾, meaning: he gathered his parents to himself. Most scholars hold that "his parents" means his father and his maternal aunt. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: it refers to his father and his mother, and she was alive. In some tafsirs: Allah the Exalted raised his mother back to life so that she came with Ya'qub to Egypt. And Allah knows best.

And His saying, ﴿And he said, "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security."﴾ The scholars differed regarding the meaning of the will (al-mashi'ah) here. Some of them said: "Enter in security from the passport (al-jawaz), ﴿if Allah wills﴾," for they would not enter Egypt before that except with a passport. It was also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, and its meaning is: "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you, if Allah wills," and he said: "Enter Egypt in security."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 100:

His saying, Most High: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾. Al-raf' (raising) is transferring to a high place, and its opposite is al-wada' (placing down). Al-'arsh (the throne) is the couch of kingship. It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The Throne shook at the death of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh." It was said: he meant by it his couch (upon which he was carried), but this is not correct, because the statement came in the description of honouring, and there is no honour in the shaking of the couch upon which he was carried. In some narrations: "The Throne of the Most Merciful shook at the death of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh." So the throne in this report is the well-known Throne, and its shaking is its rejoicing at the arrival of the soul of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. It is also permissible that what is meant, by mentioning the throne, is the people of the throne from among the angels, and Allah knows best.

And His saying: ﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾. Its meaning: they fell prostrate before him. They differed concerning this prostration. Most of them say that they prostrated to him, and the prostration was a prostration of love, not a prostration of worship, and it is like the prostration of the angels to Adam, peace be upon him. The people of knowledge said: this was permissible in the earlier nations, then Allah, Most High, abrogated it (naskh) in this law and replaced it with salam (greeting). Some of them said: they prostrated to Allah, not to Yusuf, and they bowed down before him only because he was in front of them, so their prostration was directed towards him as one prostrates towards the mihrab and the wall. The correct view is the first, so the people of knowledge have said, and the proof for it is that in his dream: ﴿Indeed, I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾, so the sun and the moon are his parents, and the eleven stars are his brothers.

If someone says: how is prostration to other than Allah permissible? And if prostration to other than Allah is permissible, why is worship to other than Allah not permissible? The answer: worship is the utmost of veneration, and the utmost of veneration is not permissible except to Allah; as for prostration, it is a kind of humble submission and lowliness through placing the cheek on the ground, and it is less than worship, so its permissibility for humans is not barred, like bowing.

Some of them said: ﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾ — prostration here is bowing, and it was expressed by the word prostration, while the true prostration did not occur. The first of the sayings is the most preferable, and Allah knows best.

His saying: ﴿And he said: O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before﴾ [Tafsir]: "my dream from before." ﴿My Lord has made it true﴾, i.e., genuine. ﴿And He has been good to me﴾, i.e., He has bestowed favour upon me, ﴿when He took me out of the prison﴾. If someone says: how did he not say "when He took me out of the well," since the trial and affliction upon him were in the well more than in the prison? The answer to this: he turned away from mentioning the well out of nobility, so that the brothers would not be embarrassed by it, and he had said: ﴿No reproach upon you today﴾, and repeating it would be reproach and blame. Also, the blessing upon him in being brought out of the prison was greater, because he was taken out of the well and made a slave, and he was taken out of the prison and made a king.

His saying: ﴿And brought you from the desert﴾. Al-badw (the desert) is an expanse of land inhabited by people of livestock with their livestock. Ya'qub and his sons were people of livestock and tents, and al-'amad are tents, so for this he said: "and brought you from the desert." His saying: ﴿After Satan had incited [discord] between me and my brothers﴾, its meaning: after Satan had corrupted between me and my brothers ﴿through envy﴾. His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾. Al-Latif is: the gentle one, and it is said the meaning of the verse is: indeed my Lord is gentle (toward whom) He wills. The reality of al-Latif is the One who conveys kindness to others gently. His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is the Knowing, the Wise﴾, its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 101:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿My Lord, You have given me [some] of the kingdom﴾. Al-mulk (sovereignty) is the extent of power held by one who has authority over governance and management. He used the word "min" (some of), which indicates partiality, because it was from the hand of the king of Egypt. It was also said that "min" here is for specification (tajnis). Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir said: Yusuf's rule lasted seventy-two years. Others said: eighty years.

And His saying: ﴿and You have taught me [some] of the interpretation of events﴾ means: the knowledge of dream interpretation.

His saying: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ means: O Originator of the heavens and the earth.

His saying: ﴿You are my Protector in this world and the Hereafter﴾ means: You are the one who manages my affairs in this world and the Hereafter.

His saying: ﴿Let me die as a Muslim﴾ means: keep me firm upon Islam at the time of death.

Qatadah said: No prophet among the prophets asked for death except Yusuf, peace be upon him. And it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "None of you should wish for death because of a harm that has befallen him, but let him say: O Allah, keep me alive as long as life is good for me, and cause me to die when death is good for me." And in the narrative: when Yusuf had his family gathered for him and God brought his parents and household to him, he longed for his Lord and said these words. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: He lived many years after this. Others said: When he said these words, a week had not passed before he died.

As for the report of the death of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, the narrators said: Ya'qub lived with Yusuf for twenty-four years in the most fortunate condition and most pleasant life. Then death overtook him, so he called his sons and said: "O my sons, what will you worship after me?" [Qur'an 2:133], which we have mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah. Yusuf, peace be upon him, instructed that he be carried to the holy land and buried beside his father Ishaq, and this was done. They said: Ya'qub lived one hundred and forty-seven years. As for Yusuf, he lived two years after his father; it was also said: more than that. Allah knows best. He died at the age of one hundred and twenty, and they buried him in the Nile of Egypt: (because the people of Egypt quarrelled over him, and the people of each quarter requested that he be buried in their quarter, hoping for his blessing; then they agreed to bury him in the Nile of Egypt) so that the water would flow over him and his blessing would reach all of them. It is reported from 'Ikrimah that he was buried on the [right] bank of the Nile, so that side became fertile and the other side became barren. So they agreed to place him in a coffin of iron — and it was said: of marble — and buried him in the middle of the Nile, and they secured that with a chain they had. Then both banks became fertile. Yusuf had instructed his brothers that when they left Egypt they should take him out with themselves. When the time of Musa came, Musa took him out with himself to the holy land and buried him near his forefathers. In the stories it is related that an old woman guided them to the grave of Yusuf, and that this old woman asked Musa to be her companion in Paradise in return, until she showed them, so revelation came to Musa to give her that.

It is narrated by al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas: When Allah the Exalted brought Ya'qub and Yusuf together, Yusuf said to him: "O father, you grieved over me until your back was bent, and you wept over me until your sight went. Did you not know that we would meet on the Day of Resurrection?" He said: "O my son, I feared that your religion would be taken from you, and then we would not meet on the Day of Resurrection."

His saying: ﴿and join me with the righteous﴾ means: from among my forefathers, and they are: Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 102:

The words of His, the Exalted: ﴿That is among the tidings of the unseen﴾ mean: among the news of the unseen.

His words: ﴿We reveal it to you﴾ mean: We convey it to you by revelation. And His words: ﴿And you were not with them when they resolved on their affair while they were scheming﴾ refer to the brothers of Joseph and their scheming when they took him away from his father. The benefit of the verse is that, since you know this, it is through Our teaching you and Our revelation to you.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 103:

As for the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And most of mankind, though you strive eagerly, are not believers﴾. It is related that the Quraysh and the Jews asked the Prophet about the story of Yusuf. When he informed them of it in a manner that accorded with what was in the Torah, and since he was not a reader (of previous scriptures), he hoped that they would embrace Islam, but they did not embrace it. He grieved over this, so Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And most of mankind, though you strive eagerly, are not believers﴾. Its meaning: most of mankind are not believers, even though you are eager for their faith.

Almighty Allah's saying: ﴿And you do not ask them for any reward for it﴾, meaning: for the conveying (of the message), ﴿any reward﴾, meaning: any payment. And His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾, meaning: an admonition to the worlds.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 105:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth﴾ means: and how many a sign. And His saying: ﴿in the heavens﴾ — the heavens (al-samawat) are the ceilings of the earth, one above another, layer upon layer. ﴿And the earth﴾ is the place where the children of Adam dwell. As for the signs in the heavens, they are as we explained before, and they are from its sun, its moon and its stars, and the revolving of the sphere (al-falak) by them, and their standing without pillars, and other than that. Some scholars have claimed that it is permissible for a person to learn the science of the stars (ilm al-nujum) to the extent that he can recognize by it the signs of the sky. As for the signs of the earth, they are also known: its trees, its plants, all that is in it, and what comes out of it. And His saying: ﴿They pass by it, and they are heedless of it﴾ means: they turn away from it while seeing it, and they do not take it as evidence for the oneness of God.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 106:

God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except that they are associators (of others with Him).﴾ If it is said: How is it possible for faith and association to coexist in one person? The answer is given in several ways. The first: its meaning is ﴿And most of them do not believe in God﴾, that is: most of them do not acknowledge God except that they are associators in their hearts and inner consciences.

The second: when the polytheists of Mecca were asked, "Who created you?" they would say, "God." When they were asked, "Who provides for you?" they would say, "God." When they were asked, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would say, "God." Yet despite this, they worshipped idols. Some of them would say that the angels are the daughters of God, and some would say that the idols are our intercessors with God. So the first statement is faith, and the faith intended is not the true reality of faith by which a person becomes a believer; rather, what is meant is what we have explained.

The third view: the meaning of their association is their association in the talbiyah (the invocation recited during pilgrimage), for they used to say: "Here I am, O God, here I am. You have no partner, except a partner who belongs to You, whom You own along with what he owns."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 107:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they then feel secure that there will not come upon them an overwhelming (ghashiyah) punishment from Allah?﴾ It was said: a portion (qit'ah) of the punishment of Allah. And it was said: a punishment that descends (muhallalah) from the punishment of Allah. And His saying: ﴿Or that the Hour will come upon them suddenly (baghtah)﴾, i.e., unexpectedly (faj'ah). Al-baghtah is the occurrence of a thing without any prior anticipation. The poet said:

(But they passed the night, and I did not know of a sudden event... and the most dreadful thing is when the sudden event (al-baghtu) surprises you.)

And His saying: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾, i.e., they do not know.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 12, verse 108:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to Allah﴾, meaning: my path (tariq). The word sabil (sabil, "way") may be used as both masculine and feminine. The poet said:
